text.p: Motorola Inc wants to create a $6.1 billion network of 72 low-orbit satellites that would enable voice, video and high-speed data links around the world for international corporations, the Wall Street Journal reported Monday.
It said the company had filed for approval with the U.S. Federal Communications Commission last month and had begun looking for potential investors.

Bary Bertiger, Motorola's corporate vice president and general manager of its satellite communications group, told the newspaper the company had been "in contact with several telecommunications companies from around the world".

Motorola expects to take four years to complete the network once it gets approval from the federal commission and other regulatory bodies for the radio spectrum that it wants for M-Star, the newspaper said.

The project would be different from Iridium, another satellite network of which the company owns 30 percent, it said. Although M-Star would be similar in structure to Iridium, it would not be detached as a separate entity as had happened to the other network of 66 satellites, the first of which is set to go into orbit next January, it added.
"We won't fund it ourselves ... but we will have fewer partners (than Iridium)," Bertiger was quoted as saying.

The newspaper said the satellites in the M-Star network would communicate with each other via laser transmission at rates of up to one gigabit or one billion bits of information per second. The speed, faster than that of Iridium, would be fast enough for a company to keep constant tabs on its accounts or merchandise on a global basis, it said.
It could also let cellular telephone operators tie their networks with a global telecommunications infrastructure, it added.
